DEF-001: creating supplier DEF-0916-095339 showed exactly four completeness warnings and no BANK_ACCOUNT_MISSING; adding an ordering address, an orders primary contact and an HK identifier through the real UI cleared them one by one down to a single PAYMENT_TERM_MISSING, proving the banner is now reachable to zero. The residual payment-term warning cannot be cleared in this environment because Business Master has zero Active Payment Terms seeded; payment term is optional by design, so this is an environment data gap, not a Supplier defect. DEF-002: supplier 404 was suspended through the real UI (version 1 -> 2), a second contact was then created through the UI so that a supplier.contact.create audit row became the newest supplier.% row, and replaying POST /suppliers/404/suspend with the original stale version 1 returned 200 with status suspended and version still 2 — the designed §476 idempotent replay. Design §476 and §1387 specify that a repeated status command already in the same target state returns current state, and a genuine replay necessarily carries a stale version, so that change would break designed idempotency and the pre-existing test at supplierLifecycleService.test.js:85. Not applied.

observations.subject: TASK-033 mutation campaign: fourteen mutations, one survived and was the author's own vacuous assertion
observations.source_ref: Each applied alone, reverted immediately, git status asserted clean between runs. Thirteen RED first time. T11 survived: re-encrypting an account with a fresh crypto_context instead of the row's own left every test green, because the assertion checked that the UPDATE's bind parameters did not contain the old context -- and crypto_context is never in that UPDATE's SET list, so the parameters never contain any context at all. The assertion held on both sides, which is the same shape REV-030 and REV-034 kept finding. Replaced with the property that actually matters: the re-encrypted ciphertext must still decrypt under the context the row stores. A first attempt at that fix was also wrong -- the chosen test account was twelve characters and GCM ciphertext length equals plaintext byte length, so the ciphertext and the IV were both twelve bytes and the buffer picked was the wrong one. Fixed by choosing a length that does not collide. The other thirteen: reject step removed, formatting set widened back to everything non-alphanumeric, formatting set narrowed to whitespace, list using SELECT *, write permission check removed, duplicate check using only the active key, cross-Supplier duplicate blocking instead of warning, warning naming the other Supplier regardless of permission, update always re-encrypting, deactivate leaving is_default set, setDefault skipping the row lock, reveal swallowing an audit failure, and the crypto type check removed.

observations.subject: TASK-033 turns T33's manual DB plaintext check into an automated scan with its own control
observations.source_ref: T33's Verification block asks for a manual DB check that the fixture plaintext appears zero times in the Bank table, the audit log and the system log. A manual check does not get done every time, so it is automated: the test reads the column list from information_schema and scans every row and every column of supplier_bank_accounts and supplier_audit_logs for a unique fixture account, reading binary columns as latin1 so a plaintext hidden in a BLOB would still be found. It runs after both a create and an update that re-encrypts. The test carries its own control -- after the two assertions it plants the plaintext into account_holder_name and requires the scanner to find it, so 'nowhere' is not just a broken scanner. The system-log half is not covered here: nothing in this service logs, and there is no log sink in the test environment to search.

observations.subject: REV-035 CHANGES_REQUESTED at 8718fa7; HD-029 was answered and neither half of the answer had shipped
observations.source_ref: Three H, four M, five L. The reviewer was precise about where they sit: the encryption, AAD, blind-index and lock-ordering work is sound, and all three blocking findings are at the boundary -- what the service rejects, how it normalizes, and what it tells the caller when it refuses. H-2 is the serious one and it reopens DEF-021: running NFKC before classification is compatibility folding, which turns a large class of content characters into pure [0-9A-Z] so they pass the reject step unseen. A sweep of U+0080 to U+1FFFF found 1225 such codepoints, and REV-034 M-2's collapse was not closed at all, only moved from the A-with-ring family to the modifier-letter and circled-letter families. Fixed by classifying on NFC and folding only the three fullwidth ASCII ranges explicitly; a re-sweep leaves two folded codepoints, both canonical equivalences, which is the intended behaviour. While fixing it the author found a second laundering path the reviewer had not reported: String.prototype.toUpperCase is not one-to-one and maps the sharp s to SS, so the case fold was narrowed to ASCII a-z. A record correction belongs with this: the half-symbol-to-12 example used in the code comment, the implementation report and HD-029's own question text does not reproduce -- NFKC maps it to one, fraction slash, two, and U+2044 is Sm, so it was always on the rejected side. The Product Owner was therefore shown an example that does not hold while the cases that do were never put to them. The decision itself stands and holds more strongly on the real cases, but the record was wrong and is corrected here. H-1: the rejection reached callers as a 500, because the crypto's TypeError was thrown inside withTransaction and the real database wrapper rethrows non-ApplicationErrors as DATABASE_TRANSACTION_FAILED -- and HD-029 was chosen on the property that a user sees the refusal and can correct it. The test missed it because the harness's fake withTransaction did not reproduce that translation. Making the fake faithful immediately exposed a second defect: a tampered row also produced an anonymous 500, so an operator could not distinguish altered data from a key missing from the ring. Now a named 422. H-3: the duplicate pre-check filtered on active status while the unique index has no status predicate, so deactivating an account and re-adding it -- the only retirement path FR-BANK-005 allows -- turned a clean 409 into an ER_DUP_ENTRY 500. Filter removed and ER_DUP_ENTRY translated, per design 2.5's statement that the database unique is the race-time backstop and the service pre-check exists only for a clearer message. M-1, M-2, M-4 and the L findings fixed. M-3 deliberately not fixed: a cross-Supplier duplicate warning is advisory by nature, the index is per-Supplier, and nothing serialises two creates under different Suppliers.

observations.subject: REV-035 remediation reverified on the final candidate
observations.source_ref: 372/372 server tests up from 367, 71/71 client, lint clean, all four DEVELOPER suites re-run on the final candidate. Nine mutations confirm the fixes discriminate: reverting NFC to NFKC, restoring the unbounded toUpperCase, dropping the pre-transaction account validation, restoring the status filter on the duplicate check, removing the ER_DUP_ENTRY translation, removing the list permission check, making the projection mask unconditionally, returning the decrypt failure as an anonymous error again, and returning 409 instead of 403 for a missing permission. All nine RED.

observations.subject: REV-036 CHANGES_REQUESTED: a guard that provably never runs, and the same fake-fidelity failure for the third time
observations.source_ref: One H, three M, five notes. The H: the ER_DUP_ENTRY translation added for REV-035 H-3 never executes in production, because MySqlDatabaseExecutor.run wraps every statement error into MySqlDatabaseOperationError with code DATABASE_OPERATION_FAILED, leaving the driver code on error.cause.code, while the guard read only error.code. Concurrent same-Supplier creates therefore still produced a 500 whose error chain carried the raw blind-index bytes. The reviewer proved the suite could not tell the difference by mutating the guard to be correct and getting 56/56 green, because the unit harness threw a raw error carrying the driver code and the integration serviceOn passed a raw mysql2 connection. This is the third instance of one failure in this task: a fake that does not reproduce a layer hides defects in that layer. First the vacuous crypto_context assertion, then REV-035 H-1 where the fake withTransaction omitted the wrapper's error translation, now the layer below that. Both fakes were corrected and an integration test was added that makes real MySQL raise the real ER_DUP_ENTRY. M-3 was also right: branching on message.includes scans user-derived bytes, since the duplicated value is the message's first component, and the format is version-dependent; now errno 1062 plus an anchored constraint-name regex. M-2: only create's INSERT was wrapped, while the pre-check is exactly what loses races. M-1: logger.warn is (event, message, context) and was called with two arguments, so the payload landed in the message slot -- and the entire justification for the named 422 is that tampering and a missing key are distinguishable in the log, which nothing tested. The reviewer independently swept the full Unicode range to U+10FFFF, wider than the author's sweep to U+1FFFF, confirmed exactly one canonical fold remains and that the argument for keeping it is sound, and confirmed no third laundering path exists. It also confirmed REV-035 M-3's acceptance was the better trade.

observations.subject: REV-036 remediation reverified; the ledger's pre-merge commit carries identical supplier source
observations.source_ref: 376/376 server tests up from 372, 71/71 client, lint clean, all four DEVELOPER suites re-run on the final candidate. Five mutations confirm the fixes discriminate: reading only the top-level error code, branching on message prose instead of the constraint name, unwrapping update's UPDATE, dropping logger.warn's context argument, and no longer recognising errno 1062. All five RED. Recording the reviewer's note about revision 156: it pinned code_commit 9000bd5, which predates the merge of main into the branch, while CI and REV-036 were at aebb6cc. That merge brought only docs/items_management changes from PR #117, so the supplier source was identical between the two and the record carried meaning -- but it should have said so rather than leaving a reader to verify it, which is what this observation now does.

observations.subject: REV-037: the previous fix introduced a new instance of the defect it closed, and the fourth fake-fidelity layer
observations.source_ref: One H, two M, three notes. The H: REV-036's M-2 fix passed a single constraint chosen from the caller's intent, but which constraint a statement violates is decided by the data. An INSERT carrying is_default = 1 can violate both the blind-index and the default-slot unique, so a blind-index collision on a create-as-default fell through untranslated to a 500 carrying the driver's message, whose first component is the raw blind index. That is the common shape of create, since a supplier's first bank account is normally made default. The author's tests covered the diagonal two cells and missed exactly the broken one; now a list of constraints and three cells. Answering the author's direct question about fake fidelity, the reviewer found the fourth layer: MySqlDatabaseOperationError extends ApplicationError and therefore carries statusCode 500, while both doubles threw a plain Error, so they failed their own ApplicationError check and re-wrapped -- production two links, doubles three. Nothing depended on it, but the new integration test happened to search both depths, which is luck rather than design. Fixed by importing and throwing the real class rather than re-describing it, which removes the class of divergence instead of the instance. Two further divergences were acted on from a list of thirteen the reviewer supplied: neither double set REPEATABLE READ, the isolation level the duplicate-race behaviour of the last three reviews depends on; and the integration double rolled back after a failed commit, which the real code deliberately refuses because the transaction's outcome is then unknown. One surviving mutation, find to findLast, was verified to be an equivalent mutant rather than a gap: an ER_DUP_ENTRY names exactly one key and the regex anchors on the closing quote, so at most one constraint can match. Confirmed empirically and noted in the code so no one later reads order into it.

observations.subject: Four times in TASK-033 a correct and a broken implementation were indistinguishable to the suite
observations.source_ref: Worth stating once, because it is the through-line of this task rather than four unrelated slips. The vacuous crypto_context assertion held on both sides. The fake withTransaction omitted the wrapper's error translation. The layer below it omitted the per-statement wrapping. And REV-037's H-1 was found by the reviewer mutating a fix to the CORRECT implementation and watching 60/60 stay green. The first three are one failure -- a double that does not reproduce what the real thing hands over -- and the fourth is a different one: the double was faithful enough by then, but the test matrix was missing a cell. Both practices are now written into the task document: a double reproduces the real class, wrapping and isolation level, importing the real thing wherever it can rather than re-describing it; and when a fix adds a discriminator, mutate it to the correct implementation and require something to go red, which is the reverse of ordinary mutation testing and catches the case where the suite never tested the thing at all. 377/377 server tests, 71/71 client, lint clean, all four DEVELOPER suites re-run on the final candidate.

observations.subject: REV-038 APPROVED at ef1ed7d, the first of four rounds with no production defect
observations.source_ref: Zero critical, zero high, one non-blocking M, three notes. REV-037's H-1 was verified two ways: the live two-flag race that previously produced a 500 leaking the driver's duplicate message now returns 409 with no leak on both flags, and restoring the broken single-constraint choice turns the new three-cell test red. The M is worth recording because of where it was: the integration double set its committed flag after awaiting commit, so a failed commit never reached it and the double rolled back -- the exact thing its own comment two lines above says it must not do, since the real code sets commitAttempted before the await. A fifth layer, inside the commit that wrote the rule about layers. Fixed by renaming to commitAttempted and moving it ahead of the await. The reviewer's mutation remains unkilled and that is stated rather than papered over: forcing a commit failure needs the real service, which is the recommendation below, and building a test suite for a double that should be deleted would be the wrong direction. The reviewer's amendment to this task's first practice is accepted and written into section 9: prefer deleting the double to improving it. Importing the real error class closed the divergence in the error value but not in the decisions around it, because the double still copies branches and copies drift. This integration test does not need a double at all -- it already talks to real MySQL, and a real MySqlDatabaseService over a real pool, about fifteen lines, would close thirteen divergences at once because there would be no second copy to be wrong. An enumerated rule will always be one property short of the next defect, which is what four rounds of this task demonstrate. It also confirmed the find/findLast equivalence argument and improved the method: an equivalent mutant and an untested branch both survive, and what separates them is whether a non-equivalent mutation on the same code goes red. Considering only constraints[0] turns two tests red, so the list's later elements are genuinely exercised.

observations.subject: REV-039 H-1: a manifest edit moved the DESIGN baseline and two records said it did not
observations.source_ref: Correction of my own records, not a new finding. I declared .github/workflows/ci.yml in the manifest's scope.approval_required_paths and described that edit as mechanical and design-neutral. It was not. The DESIGN digest is digest({module_id, requirements, design, scope, contracts, risk}) at harness_core.py:301-307, and approval_required_paths lives inside scope, so the edit moved design from e4083319 to 77ab26aa. harness_checks.py:276-289 filters reviews against a RECOMPUTED design hash, so all 38 reviews stopped counting at once, including REV-038, the APPROVED review that gated the TASK-033 merge, and APPROVAL-HD-017-DESIGN, the module's only DESIGN-kind approval. Two records asserted the opposite: implementation report 38 section 6 said 'Review binds the design hash, unaffected', and APPROVAL-HD-031-PLAN-FINAL's own source_ref said 'No requirement, design, phase, task, suite, test flag or suite argv changed.' Both false as recorded. Verified myself rather than taking the reviewer's word: state_tool.py inspect reported observed design 77ab26aa against recorded e4083319 with BASELINE_STALE, and 28 of 38 reviews bound to the recorded hash. Resolution: the Product Owner chose to revert the manifest declaration; design is back to e4083319 and state_tool.py no longer reports BASELINE_STALE on design. The report is corrected in place with the correction marked as such, and the false approval source_ref is superseded rather than rewritten. This is the fourth time this module has been bitten by a manifest edit stranding baseline-bound records; what is new is that this time the class of record affected was one I had explicitly told the Product Owner would not be affected.

observations.subject: DEV-T34-CACHE-PRIVATE: the reveal route's Cache-Control acceptance criterion is not met
observations.source_ref: Recorded deviation, approved by the Product Owner on 2026-09-21. TASK-034's verification criterion reads 'Manual header check: reveal contains Cache-Control: no-store, private and Pragma: no-cache', and design 6.6 states the same value in its reveal response example, so this is a design-level shape and not only a task checklist line (REV-040 L-1). The private token never reaches the wire: BaseRequestHandler.handle calls sendSuccess, whose first statement is res.setHeader('Cache-Control','no-store') at framework/http/apiResponse.js:21 (and :46 on the error path), and setHeader replaces rather than appends. REV-039 measured the actual value over real HTTP on a genuine 200 reveal: Cache-Control: no-store, Pragma: no-cache. My own test could not see this and could not have: it drove handler.execute directly with a fake res, stopping one call before the framework overwrites, so a test written specifically to replace a manual check was incapable of failing when the header was wrong. The Product Owner chose to record the deviation rather than change the framework, on the reasoning that RFC 9111 5.2.2.5 makes no-store strictly stronger than private - no cache of any kind may store the response - so the security property the criterion protects is already held, while meeting it literally would require editing a response path every module in the application goes through, outside this module's allowed_write_paths. Remediation: the handler no longer sets a Cache-Control it cannot deliver; Pragma stays because the framework does not touch it; and the integration test now asserts the real wire value with assert.equal rather than assert.match, deliberately, so that if anyone ever changes apiResponse.js the test goes red and this deviation is closed on purpose instead of drifting shut. Status FAIL is accurate and intended: the criterion is not met.

observations.subject: DEV-T34-EXPIRES-IN: design 6.6's reveal response includes expiresInSeconds and the implementation omits it
observations.source_ref: Recorded deviation, previously only in the narrative implementation report (REV-039 L-4). Design 6.6's reveal example carries expiresInSeconds: 30. BANK_REVEAL_RESPONSE_SCHEMA declares exactly {id, accountNumber, revealedAt} and is additionalProperties: false, so the field cannot appear. The reasoning: no server-side state corresponds to that number. The plaintext exists only inside that one response; nothing expires anywhere, and a field that implies a server-side lifetime which does not exist is worse than no field. When the UI clears it from component memory is TASK-035's concern and does not need a number from the server. REV-039 agreed with the decision and objected only to where it was written down - nothing reading the ledger or the traceability matrix knew FR-BANK-006's design shape was not implemented as written, so the next person would have re-derived it from a diff. Status FAIL records that the design shape is not implemented as written, which is the fact a reader needs; it is not an unresolved defect.

observations.subject: REV-039 remediation: nine findings, all real, all addressed
observations.source_ref: REV-039 was performed by agent-skills:security-auditor, independent and not the author, against 64ef1fc. Verdict CHANGES_REQUESTED with 2 High, 3 Medium, 4 Low. Every one was a true finding; none was a false positive. H-1 and H-2 were baseline bookkeeping around the change rather than the change itself: H-1 is recorded separately above, and H-2 dissolved when the manifest revert returned PLAN to db5296, the hash the four evidence runs already carried - but the source changed again during remediation, so all four suites were re-run at the final baseline anyway rather than relying on that coincidence. M-1 is the recorded cache-header deviation above. M-2: the new HTTP test asserted only status 403 on an unauthorised reveal, and the reviewer killed it by changing only the password - jwt-password runs assertPasswordConfirmed before the authorization policy and a rejected password is also 403, so the assertion could not tell apart the two outcomes it claimed to distinguish; it now asserts error.code === 'Forbidden'. M-3: no test performed a successful reveal or any write over HTTP, which is the direct cause of M-1; there is now a second principal holding supplier.view plus supplier.bank.view that performs a real 200 reveal and asserts the plaintext, the actual response headers and exactly one supplier.bank.reveal audit row. AC-025 and AC-026 remain uncovered at the HTTP layer because a caller holding two of the three write permissions is refused at 400 DEVICE_SIGNATURE_REQUIRED before authorization runs; that limitation is stated in the implementation report rather than left silent. L-1: the response-schema defence depends on validation.output.enabled, which nothing pinned; two assertions now pin the shipped config, and I verified they discriminate by flipping validateInProduction to false and watching the test go red. L-2: command(req) spread the request body last, over requestId, ip and the actor identity; on the route that writes the bank audit trail the body now goes first and the framework-derived fields last. L-3: two browser suites carried the secrets in redaction_env_keys with an empty env_keys, so they could never receive what they claimed to redact; the redaction entries were removed rather than env_keys added, because adding them would make an unprovisioned suite look provisioned, which is the hazard the reviewer named. L-4 is the expiresInSeconds deviation above.

observations.subject: REV-039 remediation evidence carries no key material
observations.source_ref: The four re-run evidence directories were searched for the two literal test key values and for any 43-character base64 run followed by '=': zero hits of either. Unlike the first attempt at this check on the previous evidence set, the search used literal strings rather than an unexported shell variable, so it searched for what it meant to search for. Discriminating power verified rather than assumed: planting one of the two keys into a scratch file and running the identical commands finds it by both the literal search and the base64 pattern. A sweep that has never been shown to find anything proves nothing about finding nothing.

observations.subject: REV-040 M-1: the REV-039 L-3 fix rested on a false premise and has been reverted
observations.source_ref: Correction of a remediation, not of the original code. REV-039 L-3 observed that supplier-client-ui and supplier-uat-browser carried SUPPLIER_BANK_ENCRYPTION_KEYS and SUPPLIER_BANK_LOOKUP_KEYS in redaction_env_keys with an empty env_keys, and reasoned that they would never see the variables their redaction claimed to redact. I accepted that and removed the two entries. REV-040 showed the premise is wrong, and I verified it rather than taking the second reviewer's word either: redact() at harness_runner.py:73-79 resolves each key against os.environ, the RUNNER's environment, and never touches the child's env dict, so redaction is independent of env_keys entirely. Demonstrated with both cases, because a demonstration of only the true case proves nothing: with SUPPLIER_BANK_ENCRYPTION_KEYS set in the runner's environment, redact(text,['SUPPLIER_BANK_ENCRYPTION_KEYS']) replaces the value with [REDACTED] and redact(text,['DB_PASSWORD']) leaves it in the clear. It also matters because server/src/index.js loads server/.env through dotenv, so a suite that boots the API gets the keys whatever the profile says, which is exactly the case where captured output could carry one. Removing the two entries was therefore a small net loss of protection, justified in the ledger by a statement that was false. The profile is restored to its pre-remediation content and the PLAN baseline returns to db5296. Worth naming: this is the second time in this task that I acted on a reviewer's reasoning without testing the mechanism it rested on.

observations.subject: REV-040: eight findings, all real; the High and both Mediums were bookkeeping, not product code
observations.source_ref: REV-040 was performed by agent-skills:security-auditor, independent and not the author, against 1de07da89a1fec2eb8a753f99cb9779b8f9d50cd. Verdict CHANGES_REQUESTED with 1 High, 2 Medium, 5 Low, and it confirmed all nine REV-039 findings genuinely remediated by killing each with a mutation rather than reading the diff. Nothing it attacked on the Bank HTTP surface broke: forged JWT claims are refused at 403 PERMISSION_STALE because the service re-reads the actor from the database, IDOR returns 404 with no leak, step-up brute force locks at five attempts for fifteen minutes and a correct password during the lock still returns PASSWORD_INVALID, and weakening the route policy was caught twice with the service layer still refusing. H-1: APPROVAL-HD-031-PLAN-REBIND, APPROVAL-HD-030-SCOPE-REBIND and the H-1 correction observation all asserted a Product Owner decision while no pending_decisions entry recorded it. The decisions were real and were taken in conversation, but the harness's premise is that the ledger is the record and my memory is not, so the finding is correct as stated: HD-032 and HD-033 now exist, with the costs as they were put to the Product Owner. HD-017 is the exact precedent for HD-032 and was recorded properly at the time. M-1 is the reverted L-3 fix recorded above. My history.pushState probe was correctly diagnosed as non-discriminating; the error was concluding from one failed probe that nothing could discriminate, and then writing that conclusion into a code comment and a report section as a statement of fact. M-1: a reveal resolving after unmount re-held the plaintext and armed a fresh interval on a dead component; guarded with a flag. M-2: three clearing assertions were DOM-shaped and survived mutation. Worth recording separately: after my FIRST round of fixes I re-ran all seven mutations and four still survived. The new assertions were watching the DOM or counting total timers, and both of those become true on their own when a component unmounts or a dialog closes. pending_decisions.question: REV-033 H-1: the Bank account normalizer removes only whitespace and the ASCII hyphen, so duplicate detection is bypassable. The reviewer tried sixteen characters and ten got through, including a full stop, slash, underscore and comma, three Unicode hyphen variants, and two invisible characters, U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN and U+200E LRM. The invisible pair is the sharp end: two rows whose accounts render identically on screen and in the mask carry different blind indexes, so the UNIQUE does not fire and an operator sees the same masked account twice with no explanation. Design section 4 says NFKC, trim, remove allowed separating whitespace, preserve business-valid characters, and defines no character contract, so this is a decision rather than a bug fix. Options: an alphanumeric allowlist (NFKC, uppercase, keep only 0-9A-Z); a widened separator blocklist covering Unicode Pd and Cf plus common punctuation; or the design's literal reading, whitespace only. The table is empty today so the change is free; once rows exist it means decrypting, re-encrypting and reindexing every row, because the normalized string is what gets encrypted, HMACed and measured.
pending_decisions.answer_ref: Product Owner decision on 2026-09-21: 字母數字白名單. NFKC, uppercase, keep only [0-9A-Z], reject when the result is empty or exceeds the bound. The allowlist holds because account identifiers are alphanumeric by definition (IBAN is specified as [0-9A-Z], domestic account numbers are digits), so any other character in a typed account number is formatting. Uppercasing follows from IBAN's letters being case-insensitive. A blocklist was rejected because its problem is not which ten characters it misses today but that the next new dash will miss too.

The property that makes this work is that the formatting list being incomplete no longer matters in the dangerous direction: an unlisted separator is now loudly refused, which a user sees and can correct, rather than silently altering the account.
